# Beyond Jump Scares: Crafting Psychological Horror in Film and Literature

robhestand1

November 13, 2023November 6, 2023 Directing, Screenwriting Screenwriting, Storytelling, Writing

The Foundations of Fear: Understanding Psychological Horror

At the heart of psychological horror lies the ability to invoke fear that resonates on a deeply personal level. Unlike its more overt counterparts that rely on visceral shocks, psychological horror creeps under the skin, often leaving a lingering unease that taps into the primal fears of the human psyche. It is a craft that hinges on subtlety and the power of suggestion, allowing the audience’s imagination to become an unwitting accomplice in their terror.

This genre asks more of its audience than mere reaction; it requires introspection. Films like Roman Polanski’s “Repulsion” or the understated horror of Shirley Jackson’s “The Haunting of Hill House” are exemplars of this style. These works don’t just scare; they disturb, offering a mirror to our innermost anxieties.

Screenplay Structure in Psychological Horror

In film, the screenplay’s structure is the skeleton upon which the meat of our terror is hung. To truly unsettle, one must understand that horror is rhythm as much as it is content. The classic three-act structure can be a useful framework but beware of adhering too rigidly. Psychological horror often benefits from a more fluid approach, weaving tension and release in a dance that is as unpredictable as it is unnerving.

![](https://aiinscreentrade.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/08/komododogg_a_dreamlike_sequence_of_various_iconic_movie_element_1bb6ef95-1f20-40ab-ae03-3dad7defa429.png?w=750)

Screenwriters can employ techniques such as the slow burn, where the story’s stakes and tension gradually escalate to an almost unbearable degree before culminating in a climax that is as inevitable as it is horrifying. A prime example would be the gradual unraveling of sanity in Darren Aronofsky’s “Black Swan,” which portrays a descent into madness with surgical precision.

Writing Tips for Setting the Scene

Setting the scene in psychological horror is a subtle art. The environment must breathe unease. It could be the claustrophobic corridors of Stanley Kubrick’s Overlook Hotel in “The Shining” or the oppressive small-town Americana of Stephen King’s “It,” where every locale feels tainted by an unseen malevolence. Descriptive writing, both in screenwriting and prose, should not just paint a picture; it should hint at the unseen, at the things lurking just out of sight or beyond understanding.

Writers should consider the senses and the mind. It’s not enough to describe; one must suggest. Use sensory details sparingly but potently—let the drip of a tap or the flicker of a shadow-laden light bulb carry the weight of a paragraph or a scene. The goal is to create an atmosphere thick with anticipation, where even the mundane becomes a harbinger of dread.

Writing a Screenplay with Layers of Fear

Psychological horror demands layers. It’s not the monster that we see, but the one we imagine, that truly terrifies. To write a screenplay that captures this, one must learn the art of concealment and revelation. Provide the audience with enough to fuel their fears but hold back enough to keep them guessing.

Dialogue in psychological horror must also perform a delicate ballet. It’s here, in the spoken word, that the internal can surface in subtle tells and omens. Consider the cryptic conversations in “The Witch” or the haunting monologues in “Hereditary.” These are not merely expositional; they are psychological landscapes unto themselves, echoing with the unspoken and the unspeakable.

In literature, the internal narrative provides a direct line to fear. The fractured thoughts of Edgar Allan Poe’s narrators or the stream of consciousness in Henry James’ “The Turn of the Screw” serve not only to convey plot but to fracture reality, guiding the reader into a maze of doubt and dread.

Creating Unseen Terror: The Art of Suggestion in Screenwriting and Storytelling

In the shadowy realm of psychological horror, what remains unseen often terrifies more than the grotesque spectacles that parade across the screen or page. The art of suggestion—of hinting at a horror beyond what is shown—is a powerful tool in the writer’s arsenal. It is the unseen terror that lodges itself in the imagination, where the audience’s mind becomes the canvas on which the most horrific images are painted.

Subtlety in Horror Dialogue and Description

Horror that whispers has always been more frightening than horror that screams. The former allows the reader’s or viewer’s mind to fill in the blanks, creating personalized terrors that resonate more deeply. Take, for example, the classic terror of “Jaws.” The shark is seldom seen, but its presence is always felt, its menace implied through the characters’ reactions and the chilling score. The dialogue is not about the shark’s size or its multitude of teeth; it’s about the fear of what could happen, about the implications of stepping into the water.

Screenwriters can craft fear through what characters choose to say—or what they avoid saying. In the script for “A Quiet Place”, the dialogue is sparse, which amplifies the significance of every sound and every word spoken. Descriptions should also teeter on the edge of showing too much. Like a camera lens that focuses on a character’s terrified gaze rather than the horror that provokes it, written descriptions should prioritize reaction over spectacle.

The Unreliable Narrator as a Tool for Unsettlement

An unreliable narrator can be a profound device in psychological horror, as they fracture the reality of the narrative. They are the looking glass through which distorted truths are presented, leaving audiences questioning what is real. The classic unreliable narrators like the governess in “The Turn of the Screw” or Patrick Bateman in Bret Easton Ellis’s “American Psycho” cast shadows of doubt, making the horror deeply personal and subjective.

When writing a screenplay that involves an unreliable narrator, it’s crucial to keep the audience on unstable ground. Films such as “Fight Club” or “Shutter Island” utilize this technique masterfully, with narrators whose skewed perceptions create a pervasive sense of dread that lingers even after the twist is revealed.

Crafting Characters with Psychological Complexity

Characters in psychological horror need to be more than just victims or conduits for fear—they must embody it, contribute to it. These characters should have layers of psychological complexity that feed into the horror itself. They are not merely reacting to a haunted house or a demonic presence; they are an integral part of the horror.

Consider the character of Annie in “Hereditary,” whose grief and familial tensions are as much a source of horror as the supernatural elements of the plot. Similarly, Jack Torrance in “The Shining” is not simply a man succumbing to supernatural madness; he is a deeply flawed individual whose personal demons pave the way for his downfall.

To write such characters, one must delve into the human psyche and explore themes that are universally unsettling—loss, isolation, identity, sanity. These characters often harbor dark secrets or traumas, making them unreliable in their perceptions and reactions, which, in turn, heightens the audience’s unease. Crafting these characters requires a delicate balance between revealing enough to provoke empathy and maintaining enough mystery to create suspense.

In psychological horror, the human mind is both battleground and antagonist. By employing techniques of suggestion, creating unreliable narrators, and developing psychologically complex characters, writers can weave a narrative that does more than simply scare—it haunts. It’s in the subtle play of shadows, the quiet madness echoing through dialogue, and the characters who are all too human in their faults, that true psychological horror takes form.

This nuanced approach is the essence of the genre. It’s not just about writing a screenplay or a story; it’s about choreographing an experience of terror that feels as intimate as a whisper in the dark, an experience where the terror comes not from what is written, but from what is imagined by the reader or viewer. Through the art of suggestion, writers invite audiences to confront the unknown—the most profound fear of all.

The Climactic Unraveling: Pacing and Resolution in Psychological Horror

The third act of any psychological horror is a delicate dance with the audience’s nerves, a balancing act that must maintain tension, deliver on the built-up suspense, and resolve the narrative in a way that stays true to the genre’s unsettling core. Here, the story’s pacing and resolution are pivotal, crafting a climax that can either elevate the tale to a haunting masterpiece or see it crumble into the abyss of the forgettable.

Utilizing Writing Prompts for Unexpected Twists

Unexpected plot twists are the lifeblood of psychological horror, subverting audience expectations and re-contextualizing everything that has come before. Writing prompts can be a fantastic way to break free of clichés and brainstorm such twists. One might start with a prompt such as, “Write a scene where the protagonist realizes the monster they’re fleeing from is within them.” This can lead to revelations that redefine the nature of the horror, much like in the climactic twists of films like “The Sixth Sense” or “The Others.”

When employing such prompts, it’s important to plant seeds early in the narrative. Foreshadowing is key—subtle hints that, in retrospect, make the twist feel like an inevitable part of the story’s tapestry. The best twists feel both surprising and satisfying because they align with the story’s internal logic.

Screenwriting Tips for Sustained Tension

Tension in a screenplay must build like a crescendo in a symphony, each scene adding pressure to the audience’s sense of dread. This can be achieved through various techniques such as time constraints (the ‘ticking clock’), escalating stakes, or the strategic withholding of information.

Consider the screenplay for “Se7en,” where tension mounts as the detectives get closer to capturing the killer, each sin revealing more horror. To maintain this tension, scenes are constructed to provide just enough relief to prevent audience burnout while also inserting new questions to keep them engaged.

Dialogue and pacing become critical tools here. The rhythm of the interactions, the choice of words, can ratchet up the anxiety. A well-placed line, a moment of silence, or a character’s realization can all serve as pivot points that escalate the tension.

Resolution’s Role in Psychological Horror

The resolution in psychological horror, more so than in other genres, often leaves a lingering aftereffect, a chill that trails the audience out of the theater or lingers in their thoughts long after the book is closed. It’s not about wrapping up the story with a neat bow; it’s about delivering a conclusion that resonates on an emotional, psychological level.

In psychological horror, resolution may not mean the cessation of horror. Unlike other genres where the monster is defeated, and the world is safe, psychological horror often opts for ambiguity or a bleak outcome. For instance, the unsettling conclusion of “The Babadook” respects the genre’s roots by offering resolution not through the elimination of horror but through a kind of grim understanding and coexistence.

The significance of this type of resolution is profound. It challenges the audience, forcing them to confront unsettling truths about the human condition, about fear, and about darkness that cannot simply be vanquished. It leaves them with questions, compels them to engage with the narrative beyond the confines of its medium.

The climax and resolution must carry the weight of the narrative’s psychological complexities. They must deliver on the promise of horror that is felt in the bones, horror that whispers of things half-seen, half-understood. They must unravel the narrative in such a way that the audience is left not only scared but also deeply unsettled.

In crafting the third act of a psychological horror, writers must weave together the subtleties of pacing, the sharp turns of unexpected plot twists, and a resolution that stays true to the genre’s commitment to psychological unease. It’s a delicate craft, but when executed with skill, the climactic unraveling becomes the moment where the story transcends the horror genre to become something more profound, something that does not simply scare but also haunts, disturbs, and ultimately, endures.
